lesson.title: How Water Pulls a Salt Crystal Apart
lesson.summary: Ion-dipole forces are the attraction between a charged ion and the partial charges of a polar molecule, and they are the reason ionic compounds like table salt dissolve in water.
lesson.body:
An ion-dipole force is the electrostatic attraction between a fully charged ion and the partial charges of a polar molecule's permanent dipole. This is a distinct category from the other intermolecular forces you have studied, because it involves a full unit charge (+1, +2, minus 1, and so on) rather than two partial charges attracting each other. Because a full charge is involved on one side, ion-dipole forces are generally the strongest of the common intermolecular forces, stronger than hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole forces, or dispersion forces between comparably sized species.

The dissolving of table salt, sodium chloride, in water is the textbook example, and it is worth walking through carefully because it shows the mechanism in action rather than just naming it. Solid NaCl is an ionic compound held together in a crystal lattice by strong ionic bonds, essentially electrostatic attraction between Na+ cations and Cl- anions, as you saw when studying ionic compounds. When NaCl is dropped into water, the polar water molecules, each with a partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charges on the hydrogens, surround the crystal. Water molecules orient their oxygen ends toward the Na+ cations and their hydrogen ends toward the Cl- anions. Each of these individual orientations is an ion-dipole force. As enough water molecules accumulate around an ion, their combined ion-dipole attraction becomes strong enough to overcome the ionic bonds holding that ion in the lattice, and the ion is pulled away from the crystal and surrounded by a shell of water molecules, a process called hydration or solvation.

The strength of an ion-dipole force depends predictably on a few factors. Higher ionic charge means a stronger attraction, so a doubly charged ion like Mg2+ is hydrated more strongly than a singly charged ion like Na+ of similar size. Smaller ionic radius also strengthens the interaction, because the charge is concentrated over a smaller volume and water molecules can approach more closely; this is why Li+, despite being singly charged, is hydrated unusually strongly for an alkali metal ion. On the solvent side, a larger dipole moment on the polar molecule strengthens the attraction as well, which is part of why water, with its large dipole moment and small size, is such an effective solvent for ionic compounds.

It is worth being precise about where ion-dipole forces fit conceptually. They are not what holds NaCl together as a solid; that is an ionic bond, a much stronger and different kind of interaction operating within the compound itself. Ion-dipole forces are what happens between that compound's ions and a separate polar solvent once the two are mixed. This distinction, an intramolecular ionic bond versus an intermolecular ion-dipole force, is exactly the same kind of distinction you will lean on constantly when comparing intermolecular forces to covalent bonds. Ion-dipole forces explain not only why many salts dissolve in water but also why they generally do not dissolve well in nonpolar solvents like oil or hexane, which have no permanent dipole to offer the ions in exchange for breaking apart the lattice.
